title: Division and fractions
summary: Do a division digit by digit, and see that every fraction is really a division you can turn into a decimal.
guide: A fraction is a division! {{frac:3/4}} means 3 divided by 4, just like sharing 3 loaves of bread equally between 4 people. Each person gets {{frac:3/4}} of a loaf. So the numerator is the {{term:dividend}} and the denominator is the {{term:divisor}}.

In the written method (the bus stop), the {{term:divisor}} sits outside the bracket on the left and the {{term:dividend}} goes inside. You write the {{term:quotient}} on top, above the digits, and the subtractions underneath.

Each step has three jobs. First, work out how many times the {{term:divisor}} goes into the number and write that digit on top. Next, multiply that digit by the {{term:divisor}} and write the answer underneath. Then subtract to find the {{term:remainder}}. Bring down the next digit and do it all again.

If you run out of digits but still have a {{term:remainder}}, you can keep going: put a decimal point in the {{term:quotient}} and bring down a zero, because 3 is the same as {{num:3.0}} and {{num:3.00}}. That is how a fraction turns into a decimal: {{frac:3/4}} = {{num:0.75}}.
Every digit you get right turns green. If a digit isn't right yet, it gets a dotted border so you can work it out again. If you get stuck, press "Show me this step".

engine.label-wrong: Not yet! Work this digit out again.

eighty-four.prompt: We want to share 84 conkers equally between 4 children. Work out 84 ÷ 4, filling in the boxes digit by digit.
eighty-four.hint: Look at the 8 first: how many 4s go into 8? Write it on top. Then multiply, subtract, and bring down the 4.
eighty-four.success: Well done! Each child gets 21 conkers, with none left over.
eighty-four.why: The 2 in the {{term:quotient}}: is it really worth 2 or 20? Why?
eighty-four.model: It is worth 20. The 8 in 84 means 8 tens. Sharing 8 tens between 4 children gives each child 2 tens, which is 20. Then sharing the 4 ones gives each child 1 more. So each child gets 20 and 1, which is 21.

feedback.wrong: There are still some boxes to fill. Fill them in one at a time; if you get stuck, "Show me this step" will help.

three-quarters.title: {{frac:3/4}} means 3 ÷ 4
three-quarters.prompt: Share 3 loaves equally between 4 people. 3 is smaller than 4, so nobody gets a whole loaf: that's why we've written 0 and a decimal point in the {{term:quotient}}. Now think of 3 as {{num:3.00}} and carry on dividing.
three-quarters.hint: Now you have 30 tenths. How many 4s go into 30? 7, because 7 × 4 = 28. Subtract 28 from 30, then bring down the next zero.
three-quarters.why: Why do the fraction {{frac:3/4}} and the division 3 ÷ 4 give the same answer?
three-quarters.model: If you share 3 loaves between 4 people, each person gets a quarter of every loaf. From 3 loaves that's 3 quarters, which is {{frac:3/4}}. So every fraction is the numerator divided by the denominator.

feedback.wrong: There are still some boxes to fill. Remember to bring down the next zero after each subtraction.

seven-eighths.title: {{frac:7/8}} as a decimal
seven-eighths.prompt: Turn {{frac:7/8}} into a decimal by working out 7 ÷ 8. This time every step is up to you. The decimal point appears in the {{term:quotient}} as soon as you need it.
seven-eighths.hint: There are no whole 8s in 7, so write 0 first. Then divide 70 tenths by 8; remember 8 × 8 = 64.
seven-eighths.success: Well done! {{frac:7/8}} = {{num:0.875}}. You brought down three zeros before the {{term:remainder}} became 0.
seven-eighths.why: {{num:0.875}} is very close to 1. How could you have guessed that just from the fraction {{frac:7/8}}?
seven-eighths.model: {{frac:7/8}} is only {{frac:1/8}} less than one whole, so it must be just under 1. {{num:0.875}} is only {{num:0.125}} less than 1, and {{num:0.125}} is the same as {{frac:1/8}}.

feedback.wrong: There are still some boxes to fill. If you're stuck, read the question under the division or press "Show me this step".

three-fifths.title: What decimal is {{frac:3/5}}?
three-fifths.prompt: First work out 3 ÷ 5. Then type {{frac:3/5}} as a decimal in the box below, using a decimal point, like {{num:0.5}}.
three-fifths.hint: There are no whole 5s in 3, so the {{term:quotient}} starts with 0 and a decimal point. Then divide 30 tenths by 5.
three-fifths.why: Change {{frac:3/5}} into a fraction with denominator 10. Why does it match the answer to the division?
three-fifths.model: {{frac:3/5}} = {{frac:6/10}}, which is 6 tenths, or {{num:0.6}}. The division says the same thing: 3 is 30 tenths, and 30 tenths divided by 5 is 6 tenths.

feedback.empty: Type your answer in the box, written like {{num:0.5}}.
feedback.too-big: Too big. Look at the {{term:quotient}}: it starts with 0 and then a decimal point. Include the decimal point in your answer.
feedback.too-small: Too small. The 6 goes straight after the decimal point, because it is 6 tenths, not 6 hundredths.
